title: 2026 08 26 FEC
machineSummary: FMA Interim CEO Alastair Herkes, Liam Mason, and Claire Bolingford updated the committee on the banking inquiry. FMA said its OCR pass-through dashboard, on-ramp licensing, and blockchain tokenization are progressing, but said cross-government leadership is needed on digital assets to prevent New Zealand from falling behind.

chunks.text: Get into it, if that's okay. Absolutely. Thank you very much, Chair. Thank you, members, for having us back to update you on progress in response to the inquiry's recommendations since we last were here in February. My name is Alastair Herkes. I am the Interim Chief Executive of the FMA.

There you go. With me, I have Liam Mason, Executive Director of Governance, Policy and Strategy, and General Counsel, and Claire Bolingford, who is the Executive Director of Licensing and Conduct Supervision. So we have provided a response to your earlier written questions, and we're happy to answer any questions you have.

Fantastic. I might kick off, if that's all right, and then, members, feel free to raise your hands. Thank you for your submission, and thank you for making the time today. I wish we'd probably made it a little bit longer to justify your time, but nonetheless, we are keen to continue the evolution of the banking inquiry and what hurdles may or may not stand in the way.

You touch on the sandbox work that you're doing around on-ramping and fintechs, and really encouraged by that. What are you doing to, I guess, accelerate that opportunity, understand the regulatory barriers in the market? Because obviously that's been a success, and we'd like to see more of that.

Yeah, sure. I might take this, if I may. The first pilot showed us some very interesting things, one of which is that it's the base cost of entering the regulatory sphere is very high for small to medium firms. Most of the firms that showed interest in the sandbox were startups, and the feedback we heard from them is that the fixed costs, if you like, of applying for a license, particularly when you're at the trial stage, are prohibitive. And that's why in the next phase we are developing an on-ramp, what we're calling on-ramp licensing,

a streamlined licensing solution to allow smaller firms to come into the market, into the regulatory space, so that they're not spending their time trying to find a way to avoid it, in a way that allows them to test their products. Mm-hmm. Can I just ask you a question about that? Mm-hmm. Thank you. Hello, sorry for being late.

I'm interested in the on-ramp licenses, the e-money licenses. It's a genuine question. I don't understand why we are still talking about them sort of at the similar stage to what we were in '22. Can you help us as a committee sort of understand the points of tension in the system, I guess, to be able to introduce that? For context, we've got fintechs in the market now that are looking at RBNZ's announcement that they might be able to use the term bank and thinking that will be a better route for them. But obviously they have-

Mm-hmm... to undertake a lot of services that are out of sequence for them, and if they were to grow a bit more naturally and in line with other competitors, say, in Australia, they'd be looking for your licensing. Yeah, sure. And where we're starting with the on-ramp license is the managed investment scheme license, which is something that's been in place since, operational since 2016.

But it was designed at a time when it was fairly document heavy, and designed for what I'll call mainstream managed funds. But it's actually quite a flexible type of license. So we've been out in the market over the last couple of months, testing what we're calling a straw man for that. The reason is we want to make sure that what we design actually works for the participants, rather than just being a sort of regulated design solution.

Yeah. Feedback we've got is very constructive on that, and we'll be consulting further towards the end of August on a more formed up plan for that. And can I just ask this at the moment? So as I understand it, that's more like the old system where you've got major investors, they're over a financial cap.

They don't need the same sort of disclosure because they are majors. So the products that you're building there are simply cutting out the old PDS. What is the hold-up, though, for the licenses where you've got fintechs wanting to deliver services directly for consumers and to use payments as part of their offering then?

So there have been a couple there, and we did look at that through the first phase of the sandbox, which is, we cover this in our tokenization discussion paper that we put out. New Zealand doesn't really have a regulatory way to recognize payments- Yeah... outside of banking, and what we're doing is what we can with the financial services license, which also wasn't designed for payments.

So we've found some solutions that have helped individual firms so far, such as we designated the stablecoin offered by ECDD as not a financial product, to allow that to come to market, and we think with the flexibility of the managed investment schemes, we will be able to help more small firms. It's not intended for the large investors necessarily.

The exemptions that we gave in the first part of the sandbox for some of the players were actually for very small investments to encourage retail participation. So we're hopeful that we can do the same with this. Okay. You sort of set entirely new thing. Dan? Thanks, Mr. Chair. Thanks for coming before us today and for what your team do. Just want to switch to another part of the banking inquiry around transparency.

FMA, you've got this OCR pass-through dashboard, which I've been looking at quite a lot and seeing fairly consistent decreases in time to pass through OCR reductions. I'm wanting to know if you've got any learnings from how that dashboard's working.

Has it actually resulted in, in light of transparency, has it resulted in- Greater reductions in passer of OCR reductions. And then secondly, if there's any learnings for how you can bring greater transparency to the way fees and actions are set by banks using the same principles of what you've done here. Thank you.

Thank you. Yeah. I might pick that one up, if that's okay. Thank you for the question. So yeah, the data set is just about a year old now, and so it's still relatively early days in terms of the trend analysis that we're seeing. But to your question, I think we are seeing some interesting insights in that in terms of the timing, as you say, and that varies between entities. So we can see that quite transparently.

This is what we call a sunlight mechanism, so it means everybody's got access to the data, and we think that's helpful for customers and actually for the wider community in terms of understanding what's happening. We are also seeing that new customers of floating rate mortgages do often receive interest rate changes earlier than existing customers, which is something that we're quite interested in, and we'll be exploring further in our engagement with the banks on this.

And equally, floating mortgages and on-call savings account interest rates responses don't always move together. Mm. So that's another area that we will be exploring the banks in terms of what the rationale is for that and why they have chosen to move them at different rates. So as that data set matures, we are looking to see whether it would be helpful to expand that further.

And actually, we're looking to create a little bit more as we get more data in, further kind of iterations of the dashboard, so that we can make different insights available through the dashboard. Interesting. So supplementary. So you've got a year of data. Are there any preliminary findings of that year of data in terms of banks' responsiveness to OCR changes and whether they're actually coming down, and is there any actual results that you've got within that one year of data, or it's still too early?

I think we feel it's a little too early to tell at this stage, not least because we've had different rate changes at different times. So in terms of a trend analysis, I think we feel we need a bit more time. Mm. And as I said, we will continue to engage with the banks on this topic in terms of the underlying reasons as to why they make some of those changes at different points in the cycle as well.

Okay. Wonderful. Thank you. So more to come. Adriana Williams. Just a brief question about that. I also am a fan of that tool. Why did it just sort of go on the website with zero fanfare? We would think that... This committee's very interested in it, the minister's interested in it. Was this another sign that things aren't all happy at the FMA?

What are we meant to read into something which is a massive contribution to competition, and something that's been campaigned on for a long time by members of the community, just kind of realizing it was there one day ? Yeah. Thank you. So because this is the first time that we've done something like this, we did want to what we call soft launch it. So we weren't quite sure how it was going to land.

And also, some of the participation in it is voluntary as well, so we wanted to make sure that we got the data- Oh... sets quite tight for that before we actually made more of the information that was there. It's really important that when we're putting things out publicly, we make sure the data's accurate and is good quality.

And so that's why last year when we launched it, we wanted to ensure that we had the right quality controls over that before we publicized it more widely. What's- Thanks, Todd. Sorry. Let's keep moving. Oh, yeah. My question's a slightly different one. Obviously, in our report also, we identified the Council of Financial Regulators as an important body.

And obviously, Dr. Brenner has presented to us just in the last few weeks in her role as the co-chair. I suppose I'm just keen to get some assurance, because is that now you, Mr. Hircis, acting? Because all I want to just understand is we don't want to lose momentum on the work that is being taken there.

And again, it's probably not the right forum today to go into, let's just say, the changes at the FMA and some of the uncertainty. But I just want to, I suppose, get your reassurance that one, are you going to be, in your acting role, you're also the acting co-chair of COFA, and are you across the work programming, and can the FMA continue to support that work?

Well, thank you, Mr. Stevenson. Yes. As part of my role as interim CEO, I will be stepping into the role of being one of the co-chairs, I believe, of COFA alongside Dr. Bremner. Yes. And the organization as a whole is fully supportive and up-to-date in terms of the work program.

And so I will be- Yeah. Sure... able to be fully participating in that and fully briefed. The first meeting coming up of the heads is about four weeks away. Yeah. And so I will be attending that fully briefed and with a colleague as well. So we will be continuing our participation.

That's good to hear. And then just a quick supplementary. Obviously, the other thing Dr. Bremner touched on is obviously trying to use the COFA to actually coordinate the requirements on all of the people in the financial services sector. And so from the FMA's point of view, have you made progress on coordinating what you're going to be requiring of people and making sure, seeing how that fits in, and yeah. What kind of visibility have you got of that now?

I might ask Liam to give a specific- Yeah... couple of examples. We mentioned a couple of those when we last appeared before you. Mm. But working with the Reserve Bank team to coordinate our frontline supervision, which Claire obviously leads, and the information request there. One example was the recent work on insurance affordability.

Yeah. Used that COFA connection to make sure that we had streamlined information requests to make that as manageable as possible for the firms. So yes, that's ongoing work for us. Thank you. I'll combine two questions into one, if I could. In terms of fintech innovation, you've got blockchain tokenization that I know you've done your paper on.

Blockchain obviously knocking on your door, they're knocking at everyone's door. Yeah. Are we at the risk of falling behind Australia and Singapore in terms of regulation? Is one of my questions, and I know that you guys are sort of pioneering in some of that space. But I'd also like to know, do you need legislative political leadership or direction in terms of legislation, or have you got a sufficient remit within your purview as FMA and the Reserve Bank to enable and catalyze some of that ecosystem?

Sure. Thank you. One of the themes that came through very strongly in the submissions on our tokenization paper was the lack of a coherent cross-government regulatory regime in New Zealand for digital assets, for tokens, and for blockchain.

We believe that we can continue to make progress using the powers that we've got. But one of the things that we said in our response to submissions is that we will continue to work with government, looking for a cross-government response, yes. Is it just bubbling away on the never, never, or have you got milestones where there's going to be regulatory certainty because that's what the market's really seeking?

The certainty is absolutely what the participants want, and we can provide that within our space. But I think that there is some exploratory work that COFA's looking at, and that I think will help us to get a roadmap that we need for the cross-government solution, because we don't have it at this point.

I guess I'm about to go to Aruna to finish up, but I guess the risk is that, yeah, we're doing some work, FMA is doing some work, COFA's doing some work, Reserve Bank's doing some work, MBIE's doing some work. Meanwhile, Singapore's moving miles ahead, Australia's moving miles ahead-... and billions of dollars of bypassing New Zealand's market. So I guess, what do you need, or what do you need to do to sort of lock some of this in?

One of the things that we think we do need is to bring together the different parts of government for that, and some of the work that we're doing at the moment is thinking about what will need to be in briefings for incoming ministers after the election. Because certainly what we're hearing from the fintech industry is there is a very real risk of us falling behind. Yes.

So I guess, go back to my first question, does it need political leadership to help you in that? Does the twain need to meet? That's what he's saying. I think it is going to need government leadership, yes. Okay, thank you. Aruna. Your junk insurance report was great. Thank you for that work. I cannot think of a clearer breach of COFI than 2% loss ratio on these insurance products. Why aren't you prosecuting?

So the report that we've done is to effectively show insights from the industry. So we have done, as you'll have seen from that, a lot of monitoring activity over the course of the last year. We did see some- We should know... we did see some good practices from the industry. We- And we are following up in those areas where we see poor practices as well.

That's the one thing. Okay. The end. Thank you for coming in. Appreciate it. Thank you, members. It was short- Thank you... but appreciate those insights. And thank you for the work you're doing and all the best with the work ahead of you. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, members. Trust
